bull_bear.title: Management commentary

bull_bear.body:
- **GRM volatility** — refining margins swing with crude–product spreads and global supply/demand.
- **Marketing-margin / pricing risk** — auto-fuel marketing margins can compress when retail prices lag crude spikes (administered-pricing / political sensitivity for a PSU OMC).
- **Subsidy / LPG under-recovery** — domestic LPG (and any cooking-fuel under-recovery) can weigh on cash flows pending government compensation.
- **Leverage from large capex + working capital** — sizeable refinery/petchem/transition capex plus crude-inventory and receivable working-capital swings pressure debt and coverage.
- **Energy-transition risk** — long-run demand shift away from fossil transport fuels; execution risk on green-H2/EV/biofuel investments.
- **FX / crude price** — foreign-currency borrowing and crude import dependence expose IOC to rupee and oil-price moves.
bull_bear.title: Key risks

bull_bear.body:
- Extensive nation-wide infrastructure network across refining, pipelines and marketing that enabled uninterrupted supply through the West Asia crisis and Strait of Hormuz disruptions
- Market leadership in India's downstream oil business, with highest-ever domestic petroleum sales of 88.97 MMT in 2025-26 versus 84.96 MMT the previous year
- Largest retail distribution reach: 2,635 new retail outlets commissioned during the year taking the total network to 42,818 outlets as of March 31, 2026, plus a CNG network of 2,641 stations and over 15,000 EV charging / battery-swapping locations
- Refinery operating flexibility - refineries ran at 107.4% of installed capacity with highest-ever crude throughput of 75.45 MMT, and were re-optimised to process alternative crude grades when Middle Eastern grades were displaced
- Best-ever energy efficiency: refinery Energy Intensity Index of 90.1 and MBN of 65.7, with Mathura and Panipat entering the top quartile of the Solomon Energy Benchmark for the first time
- Integrated and diversified value chain spanning refining, pipelines, petrochemicals, natural gas, CGD, alternative energy, E&P, explosives and cryogenics
- Diversified crude and LNG sourcing capability - spot LNG cargoes procured from the USA, Angola, Indonesia, Trinidad & Tobago, Nigeria and Oman during the Strait of Hormuz disruption
- Centralised group treasury through the GIFT City platform (IOC Global Capital Management IFSC Ltd), with cumulative financial transactions exceeding USD 1 billion across India, the US, Singapore, UAE, Sri Lanka and Mauritius till 2025-26
- Highest-ever liquid pipeline throughput of 102.52 MMT, surpassing the previous record of 96.92 MMT in 2024-25
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Rising geopolitical risk and disruption of critical energy corridors — Geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, sanctions and disruptions across critical energy corridors influence global energy markets. Developments in West Asia and around the Strait of Hormuz - through which nearly 20% of global oil and LNG trade flows - drove volatility across crude oil, natural gas, freight and insurance markets. The Directors' Report states directly that despite excellent FY26 performance, 'escalation of geopolitical disruptions may have an adverse impact on profitability of 2026-27', and that the fag end of 2025-26 saw prolonged disruptions to the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz and significant dislocations in global supply chains for petroleum products and LPG.
- High import dependence and supply-security concentration — India's crude oil import dependence has increased to around 88%, and growing gas demand is expected to raise LNG import requirements over the medium term. Dependence on imported crude oil, LNG, petrochemical feedstocks and critical minerals exposes the business to supply concentration risk, currency fluctuation and external market disruption - raising the importance of diversified sourcing, resilient logistics and long-term supply arrangements. Crude sourcing, supply-chain continuity and foreign exchange exposure are named as key risks the Company actively managed during the year.
- Energy price volatility and margin uncertainty — Global energy markets are increasingly characterised by short-term price volatility rather than stable pricing cycles. The correction in India's gas consumption during H1 2025-26, driven by elevated LNG spot prices, demonstrated how sensitive demand is to commodity prices. Such volatility influences procurement strategies, inventory management, project economics and capital-allocation decisions - directly relevant for a company whose refining margins are also listed among the key risks managed during the year.
- Petrochemical margin pressure from global oversupply — Large-scale petrochemical capacity additions in China and the Middle East continue to pressure global utilisation rates and margins. Naphtha-based producers - which is IndianOil's position - remain exposed to feedstock cost volatility and to competition from gas-based producers benefiting from lower-cost ethane and LPG feedstocks. Prolonged oversupply may continue to affect profitability across commodity petrochemical value chains, a structural headwind against the Company's petrochemical expansion strategy.
- Policy, regulatory and energy-transition risk — The energy transition brings stricter environmental regulations, carbon-related trade measures, fuel-quality requirements and disclosure obligations. Emerging frameworks on emissions, carbon intensity, sustainable fuels, shipping and industrial decarbonisation may increase compliance requirements, affect competitiveness and require additional investment in cleaner technologies and operating systems.
- Climate, weather and system-resilience risk — Increasing frequency and intensity of heatwaves, floods and other climate events present operational and infrastructure risks across the energy value chain. Rising cooling-driven electricity demand, pressure on power systems and weather-related disruptions increase the need for resilient infrastructure, storage and operational flexibility; rapid renewable expansion also requires continued investment in transmission, balancing mechanisms and grid stability.
- Changing global trade flows, emerging energy blocs and critical-mineral / technology supply-chain dependence — Regional supply alliances, export controls, sanctions and strategic competition across energy technologies may alter trade flows, investment patterns and technology access. Separately, the shift toward batteries, renewables, electrolysers, semiconductors and digital infrastructure increases dependence on critical minerals whose global supply chains (lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths, batteries, clean-energy equipment) remain highly concentrated geographically - a new form of strategic vulnerability, trade risk and price uncertainty for IndianOil's transition investments.
- GOVERNANCE / OVERSIGHT GAP - board risk committees discontinued for want of Independent Directors — This is a company-specific structural risk disclosed in the Directors' Report itself. The Company has an ERM framework and constituted a Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board, but 'due to non-availability of any Independent Director on the Board, the RMC has been discontinued w.e.f. March 28, 2026', as was the Audit Committee. Board-level risk oversight now rests on the management-level Risk Management Compliance Board (senior management personnel headed by the Chief Risk Officer), because changes to the Risk Register require RMC approval and periodic updates go to the Audit Committee and Board. Appointment of directors vests with the Government of India through MoP&NG, so remediation is outside the Company's control.
- Fraud and internal-control incidents at operating locations — 7 instances of suspected fraud by employees were reported during the year. Three were below Rs 1 Crore (POL pilferage through tank trucks of Rs 19.04 Lakh at Panipat Marketing Complex; Rs 39.17 Lakh of vendor-bill splitting to bypass approvals at North Guwahati Bottling Plant; Rs 39.60 Lakh of fraudulent vendor/contractor payments at Chittoor Terminal). Four exceeded Rs 1 Crore and were reported by the Statutory Auditors to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (POL pilferage of Rs 1.37 Crore at Kandla FST; Rs 1.41 Crore via manipulation of dip measurements at Pathankot AFS; Rs 1.53 Crore of fraudulent vendor payment at Gujarat Refinery; Rs 6.00 Crore of fraudulent payment to engineering contractors under Karnataka State Office). Investigations and disciplinary action are ongoing in some cases. The recurring pattern - product pilferage and circumvention of procurement/payment procedures across dispersed terminals, bottling plants and refineries - is a structural control risk for an asset- and location-dispersed distribution business.
- Open C&AG audit paras — As on March 31, 2026 there were twenty-two pending C&AG audit paras from performance, compliance, thematic and proprietary audits, on subjects including short realisation from disposal of land, an abandoned E&P project, grade-wise costing of petrochemicals, extra cost from delay in tender finalisation, PMUY benefits to unentitled persons, avoidable entry tax, updation of daily price change at retail outlets, recovery of turnover tax, expenditure turning infructuous from non-adherence to pollution clearance requirements, spectrum utilisation, MSME procurement, infructuous expenditure on a low-hydrocarbon and risky E&P block, supply logistics of petroleum products, idle investment in plant, infructuous expenditure on financing an inoperative pipeline, and various employee-benefit matters. Offsetting this, the C&AG issued NIL comment on the FY26 supplementary audit - the 20th consecutive year - and the Auditors' Report contains no qualification or adverse remark.
- Operational safety, cybersecurity and regulatory compliance — Explicitly named by the Board among the key risks proactively managed during the year, alongside crude sourcing, supply-chain continuity, forex exposure and refining margins. The Company cites cyber threats as a feature of its operating environment and manages these through its diversified sourcing strategy, infrastructure network and continuous monitoring mechanisms, supported by an internally developed ERM portal for enterprise-wide risk tracking.

business.body:
Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOC / "IndianOil") is India's largest integrated oil & gas company and a Maharatna PSU majority-owned by the Government of India. It operates across the full downstream value chain: crude refining, petroleum-product marketing (fuel retail + bulk/industrial + LPG/aviation), a large cross-country pipeline network, petrochemicals, natural gas, and an expanding new-energy portfolio (green hydrogen, EV charging, biofuels/ethanol, batteries). It is the flagship national oil-marketing company (OMC) alongside BPCL and HPCL.

outlook.body:
- Balance core growth with new energy investment - management explicitly frames refining expansion, petrochemical integration and investments in renewables, green hydrogen and SAF as competing demands on financial capital, and allocates capital between businesses serving India's current energy demand and emerging energy pathways.
- Deepen refinery-petrochemical integration and move up the value chain into high-value petrochemicals - the Acrylics and Oxo-Alcohol project at Gujarat Refinery marks entry into high-value petrochemicals and strengthens downstream integration.
- Import substitution and Atmanirbhar Bharat - several new polymer grades and specialty petrochemical products were introduced during the year to reduce import dependence; post-commissioning of the Butyl Acrylate facility, imports of Butyl Acrylate declined by 23%.
- Crude basket diversification to reduce dependence on traditional sources - seven new crude grades added during the year, taking the portfolio to 275 crude grades sourced from 48 countries, enhancing supply flexibility and resilience.
- Build clean-energy production capability aligned with the Net-Zero roadmap and the Government's National Green Hydrogen Mission - India's first large-scale 10 KTPA green hydrogen plant at Panipat, plus ISCC CORSIA certification at Panipat for Sustainable Aviation Fuel production.
- Grow pipeline-based transportation efficiency and revenue, including through joint venture companies (IHB Ltd., Kochi Salem Pipelines Pvt. Ltd. and Indradhanush Gas Grid Ltd.).
- Add capacity while managing resource intensity - additional refining and petrochemical capacity raises the importance of energy efficiency, asset reliability and responsible resource use across a larger operating footprint.
- Invest in R&D, proprietary technologies and energy efficiency for better asset economics (stated trade-off 03; the routed text is truncated mid-sentence here).
- Sustain downstream marketing leadership through disciplined marketing strategies, supply-chain resilience, digital enablement and customer-centric initiatives, with continued retail outlet network expansion.
- The Company has a Board-formulated Dividend Distribution Policy, listed among its well-defined corporate governance policies and hosted on the Company's website; dividends declared/recommended are stated to be in accordance with that policy. Alongside it the governance framework names a Policy for determining Material Subsidiaries, a Policy on Materiality of Related Party Transactions, a Policy for dealing with unclaimed amounts towards Interest/Dividend/Redemption on listed non-convertible securities, an Enterprise Risk Management Policy, a Whistle Blower Policy, an Integrity Pact, a Code of Conduct for Board Members and Senior Management, a Code for Prevention of Insider Trading, a Sustainability & CSR Policy, a Policy for determination and disclosure of Material Event/Information and a Policy for Preservation of Documents. The only allocation ACTION visible in this routed text is the ordinary business item at the 67th AGM to declare a final dividend of Rs 1.25 per equity share for 2025-26. Note that the routed text does NOT contain the substantive dividend policy itself - see extraction notes. As a Government Company under MoP&NG the appointment of directors, and by extension board-level oversight of capital allocation, rests with the Government of India.
- Net-Zero commitment by 2046 - the Directors' Report states the Company's strategy of integration, diversification and capability building is 'aligned with the Company's long term Net-Zero commitment by 2046'.
- BRSR published annually, aligned with the 9 principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct; in line with the SEBI Master Circular the BRSR Core KPIs have been reasonably assured by Bureau Veritas (India) Pvt. Ltd., and the BRSR is hosted at https://www.iocl.com/business-responsibility-report.
- A separate third-party assured Sustainability Report is published in alignment with GRI standards.
- Enterprise Risk Management framework covering environmental and climate-related risks alongside strategic, operational, financial, legal, compliance, technological and reputational risks, supported by an internally developed ERM portal; a Risk Management Compliance Board headed by the Chief Risk Officer periodically reviews the risk profile.
- Governance and ethics infrastructure: a Vigilance function linked to the Central Vigilance Commission - 296 Vigilance Awareness programmes covering approximately 13,649 stakeholders and 26 specialised training programmes for 115 vigilance functionaries during 2025-26; 1,223 complaints processed of which 1,084 were disposed of; 278 vigilance-related disciplinary cases disposed of.
- POSH (Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013) compliance with Internal Committees across all Units/Regions/Head Office headed by senior-level women employees: 3 complaints pending as on 1st April 2025, 7 received and 7 disposed of during 2025-26, 3 pending as on 31st March 2026 of which 2 were pending for more than 90 days; regular awareness workshops for women employees and gender-sensitisation programmes for male employees.
- Internal Financial Controls framework with a dedicated Internal Audit Department headed by an Executive Director reporting to the Chairman, carrying out risk-based audits across business units; the Board states the systems provide reasonable assurance and are operating efficiently.

outlook.body: IndianOil is running an infrastructure expansion programme anchored on three strategic pillars - Strengthening Core Businesses, Accelerating Green & Clean Energy, and Embracing Future-Ready Diversification. Capital expenditure of Rs 32,405 Crore (including equity investments of Rs 663 Crore) was incurred during 2025-26, a figure the Company says has grown nearly 2.2 times over the past decade. Over 170 projects, each with capex exceeding Rs 5 Crore, are in various stages of execution with a cumulative capex of over Rs 2.5 Lakh Crore, undertaken on a standalone basis as well as through joint ventures and subsidiaries, to be financed through a prudent mix of internal accruals and borrowings. In REFINING, multiple brownfield expansion and integration projects are under implementation with the objective of raising commissioned group refining capacity from 80.75 MMTPA currently to around 98 MMTPA by 2027-28; the major expansion projects at Panipat, Gujarat and Barauni refineries, plus the PX-PTA complex at Paradip, are described as progressing well. In PETROCHEMICALS, the Rs 5,894 Crore Acrylics/Oxo-Alcohol Complex at Gujarat Refinery, a 153 KTPA Butyl Acrylates complex and a 260 KTPA Group-III base oil project at Haldia Refinery are intended to build presence in specialty chemicals, premium lubricant base stocks and high-value downstream products. In PIPELINES, key projects under implementation include the 2,730 km Kandla-Gorakhpur LPG Pipeline through a joint venture (among the world's longest LPG pipeline systems), conversion of the Mundra-Panipat Pipeline linked to refinery expansion, and the Kochi-Kanyakumari-Thoothukudi natural gas pipeline for southern India; the network is being augmented with over 1,600 km of new capacity, alongside storage infrastructure, automation and preparation for the Government's CBG blending programme. In MARKETING, the retail network of over 42,800 outlets is being expanded and repositioned into an integrated multi-energy mobility ecosystem through Transformative Retail Outlets, CPCL's 'Sooper' branded outlets, 'Apna Ghar' facilities (378) and Wayside Amenities (87), EV charging, CBG dispensing and non-fuel retail. In LPG, infrastructure expansion includes the Kandla-Gorakhpur LPG Pipeline, new bottling plants and supply infrastructure in remote and underserved regions. In GAS, the Company is expanding LNG sourcing/trading, regasification, CGD, Auto LNG and industrial gas. In UPSTREAM, it is expanding domestic and overseas exploration blocks. In GREEN & CLEAN ENERGY, construction has commenced on India's first large-scale 10 KTPA Green Hydrogen Plant at Panipat Refinery; a 100 KTPA HEFA-based SAF plant at Paradip Refinery is planned through a proposed joint venture structure; JV IndianOil NTPC Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. is on course to commission 50 MW of RE capacity this year against a planned 650 MW round-the-clock renewable power requirement for refinery expansion projects; 467 retail outlets were solarised during the year taking the total to 36,341 outlets and ~180 MW of installed solar at retail; and under SATAT the Company held 559 active CBG Letters of Intent with 49 plants established including 5 commissioned during the year. Terra Clean Ltd (TeCL) has land aggregation under progress in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh and achieved an 'AA' credit rating from CARE. Water infrastructure is being extended - treated wastewater already supplied to Mathura Refinery from an 8 MLD STP and Gujarat Refinery from a 20 MLD STP, with plans to extend a similar arrangement to Haldia Refinery through a 3 MLD STP by 2027-28.

outlook.body:
- India is expected to remain the largest contributor to incremental global oil demand over the next decade, with demand projected to increase from about 5.5 mb/d to nearly 8 mb/d by 2035, and India's overall energy requirement expected to more than double by 2050 - supporting long-term opportunities across refining, marketing, pipelines, petrochemicals, natural gas, aviation fuels and downstream infrastructure.
- In India, petroleum product demand has grown at a CAGR of 5.6% over the last five years; domestic petroleum product consumption rose 1.7% to 243.2 MMT in 2025-26, with Motor Spirit up 6.5% to 42.6 MMT and High-Speed Diesel up 3.6% to 94.7 MMT.
- Transport and aviation fuel growth: rising vehicle ownership, road infrastructure, freight movement; ATF consumption reached a record 9.16 MMT, up 2.0% and over 8% above pre-pandemic levels; India is among the world's fastest-growing aviation markets.
- Petrochemical import-substitution headroom: India depends on imports for nearly 45% of its petrochemical requirements and per capita consumption at around 15 kg is roughly one-third of the global average; domestic capacity is projected to reach about 55 million tonnes by 2035 and the market to expand to USD 375 billion by 2027 and nearly USD 1.25 trillion by 2040.
- Gas-based economy expansion: gas demand projected to approach 135 bcm by 2035, supporting investment across LNG sourcing, regasification, pipelines, CGD and downstream infrastructure; CGD remains a key growth segment supported by network expansion and rising CNG adoption. FY26 saw a temporary correction - consumption fell an estimated 3.9% to around 68.5 bcm on elevated H1 spot LNG prices - but the medium-term outlook remains constructive as prices ease and new LNG supply comes online.
- Electrification: global electricity demand projected to increase by over 40% by 2035; India added a record 51 GW of renewable capacity and 3.7 GW of large hydro in FY 2025-26 to reach 274.7 GW total, against a target of over 600 GW by 2032; renewable generation up 22% to 310 TWh, share of generation up from 13.9% to 16.8%.
- EV adoption as both an opportunity and a demand headwind: EV registrations exceeded 2.5 million units in FY 2025-26 with penetration rising to 8.5% from 7.7%; electric two-wheelers were nearly 58% of EV sales and electric passenger vehicles grew approximately 86%; public charging infrastructure expanded to more than 27,000 stations, supporting multi-energy retail formats.
- Digitalisation, AI and data-centre-led energy demand creating incremental opportunities across power supply, cooling fuels, lubricants, gas-based backup systems and renewable integration.
- Shipping and marine fuels: India's growing trade volumes, expanding port infrastructure and strategic location support marine fuels, LNG bunkering and lubricants; lower-emission shipping fuel adoption supports LNG, biofuels and green methanol demand.
- Policy tailwinds: National Green Hydrogen Mission with an outlay of Rs 19,744 Crore (green ammonia auctions, refinery hydrogen projects, incentives for 3,000 MW p.a. of electrolyser manufacturing, hydrogen hubs) and the National Critical Minerals Mission (Rs 7,280 Crore rare-earth magnet programme and a Rs 1,500 Crore recycling scheme). Ethanol blending in petrol achieved the 20% national target by March 2026.
- Structural India context: fossil fuels account for nearly 93% of total primary energy supply; India is the world's third-largest energy consumer; installed refining capacity of 258.1 MMTPA makes it the second-largest refining hub in Asia and fourth globally, with refinery throughput up 1.3% to 272.1 MMT.
- THREAT - rising geopolitical risk and supply disruption: West Asia developments and the Strait of Hormuz, through which nearly 20% of global oil and LNG trade flows, drove volatility across crude, gas, freight and insurance markets; product imports fell 7.9% to 46.8 MMT and exports fell 5.6% to 61.4 MMT on cargo rerouting and logistical constraints.
- THREAT - high import dependence: India's crude oil import dependence has increased to around 88% (crude imports up 0.9% to 245.4 MMT while domestic crude production fell to 28 MMT from 28.7 MMT), and growing gas demand is expected to raise LNG import requirements, exposing the sector to supply concentration risk, currency fluctuation and external disruption.
- IHB Ltd. (joint venture) is in advanced stages of completion of the approximately 2,800 km long Kandla-Gorakhpur LPG Pipeline.
- Indradhanush Gas Grid Ltd. (IGGL) commissioned the 392 km Guwahati-Numaligarh pipeline section of the over 1,600 km long North-East Gas Grid (NEGG) project - the balance of the NEGG remains under execution.
- Kochi Salem Pipelines Pvt. Ltd. is cited as a joint venture supporting long-term pipeline growth (no status detail given in the routed text).
- Construction of India's first large-scale 10 KTPA Green Hydrogen Plant at Panipat Refinery & Petrochemical Complex commenced after issuance of LOA on 26th June 2025 to L&T Energy Green Tech Ltd. on a Build-Own-Operate basis with a long-term supply arrangement of 25 years.
- Several major revamp and augmentation projects across refineries - hydrogen unit, sulphur recovery unit, coker LPG Merox, revamped effluent treatment facilities and tankage expansion - progressed substantially during the year.

risks.note: Geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, sanctions and disruptions across critical energy corridors influence global energy markets. Developments in West Asia and around the Strait of Hormuz - through which nearly 20% of global oil and LNG trade flows - drove volatility across crude oil, natural gas, freight and insurance markets. The Directors' Report states directly that despite excellent FY26 performance, 'escalation of geopolitical disruptions may have an adverse impact on profitability of 2026-27', and that the fag end of 2025-26 saw prolonged disruptions to the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz and significant dislocations in global supply chains for petroleum products and LPG.
risks.risk: Rising geopolitical risk and disruption of critical energy corridors

risks.note: India's crude oil import dependence has increased to around 88%, and growing gas demand is expected to raise LNG import requirements over the medium term. Dependence on imported crude oil, LNG, petrochemical feedstocks and critical minerals exposes the business to supply concentration risk, currency fluctuation and external market disruption - raising the importance of diversified sourcing, resilient logistics and long-term supply arrangements. Crude sourcing, supply-chain continuity and foreign exchange exposure are named as key risks the Company actively managed during the year.
risks.risk: High import dependence and supply-security concentration

risks.note: Global energy markets are increasingly characterised by short-term price volatility rather than stable pricing cycles. The correction in India's gas consumption during H1 2025-26, driven by elevated LNG spot prices, demonstrated how sensitive demand is to commodity prices. Such volatility influences procurement strategies, inventory management, project economics and capital-allocation decisions - directly relevant for a company whose refining margins are also listed among the key risks managed during the year.
risks.risk: Energy price volatility and margin uncertainty

risks.note: Large-scale petrochemical capacity additions in China and the Middle East continue to pressure global utilisation rates and margins. Naphtha-based producers - which is IndianOil's position - remain exposed to feedstock cost volatility and to competition from gas-based producers benefiting from lower-cost ethane and LPG feedstocks. Prolonged oversupply may continue to affect profitability across commodity petrochemical value chains, a structural headwind against the Company's petrochemical expansion strategy.
risks.risk: Petrochemical margin pressure from global oversupply

risks.note: The energy transition brings stricter environmental regulations, carbon-related trade measures, fuel-quality requirements and disclosure obligations. Emerging frameworks on emissions, carbon intensity, sustainable fuels, shipping and industrial decarbonisation may increase compliance requirements, affect competitiveness and require additional investment in cleaner technologies and operating systems.

Increasing frequency and intensity of heatwaves, floods and other climate events present operational and infrastructure risks across the energy value chain. Rising cooling-driven electricity demand, pressure on power systems and weather-related disruptions increase the need for resilient infrastructure, storage and operational flexibility; rapid renewable expansion also requires continued investment in transmission, balancing mechanisms and grid stability.

Regional supply alliances, export controls, sanctions and strategic competition across energy technologies may alter trade flows, investment patterns and technology access. Separately, the shift toward batteries, renewables, electrolysers, semiconductors and digital infrastructure increases dependence on critical minerals whose global supply chains (lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths, batteries, clean-energy equipment) remain highly concentrated geographically - a new form of strategic vulnerability, trade risk and price uncertainty for IndianOil's transition investments.
risks.risk: Changing global trade flows, emerging energy blocs and critical-mineral / technology supply-chain dependence

risks.note: This is a company-specific structural risk disclosed in the Directors' Report itself. The Company has an ERM framework and constituted a Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board, but 'due to non-availability of any Independent Director on the Board, the RMC has been discontinued w.e.f. March 28, 2026', as was the Audit Committee. Board-level risk oversight now rests on the management-level Risk Management Compliance Board (senior management personnel headed by the Chief Risk Officer), because changes to the Risk Register require RMC approval and periodic updates go to the Audit Committee and Board. Appointment of directors vests with the Government of India through MoP&NG, so remediation is outside the Company's control.
